text: Hey everybody, the concept of creation ex nihilo,  or out of nothing, is post-biblical. It's not   found anywhere in the Bible. It's an innovation  of the second century CE, and specifically,
it developed within debates between Christians and  others about the rationality of the resurrection.   And there were two things that were in view  in this discussion: one, according to the
conventional Greco-Roman wisdom of the time,  matter existed apart from deity. It was less than
deity. It was not eternal, and so the notion of  an eternal material resurrected body existing
with deity was nonsensical. Additionally, bodies  decompose. They could be consumed by other bodies,
and then expelled as waste, and so the idea that  this body could be reconstituted in anything
approximating the same body that existed  before was also nonsensical. And christians
countered this in a bunch of different ways,  but ultimately they came up with the idea that
matter is not separate from deity – matter is a  product of deity; that God is responsible for the
creation of all matter, and therefore it belongs  to God. It can be divine, it can be eternal.
And this required asserting that the whole  universe was created out of nothing, which was a
direct rejection of more conventional Greco-Roman  wisdom about nothing being able to come out of
nothing, but that was a handy christian identity  marker and also allowed them to say, "Our God
is bigger than your philosophies." Now, two texts  that are frequently cited from the Bible as being
direct indications of creation out of nothing are  Genesis 1:1 and 2 Maccabees 7:28. Neither of these
actually promotes that idea of creation out of  nothing, however. They can be better situated
within existing cosmological worldviews that  did not appeal to creation out of nothing.
The scholarly consensus regarding Genesis 1 –  the whole chapter not just the first verse – is
that it points to creation out of existing  material, and that holds even if we accept the
traditional rendering of Genesis 1:1 as, "In the  beginning, God created the heavens and the earth."
Now, a more likely rendering that does away with  some of the grammatical problems is, "When god
began to create the heavens and the earth, the  earth was tohu vavohu." And this is a poetic
couplet that is probably not used so much for any  kind of semantic specificity as for the rhyme.
It probably means something like – Robert Alter  renders "welter and waste," suggesting it refers
to kind of the trackless expanse of the desert. In  other words, it does not have a recognizable form
or function, but it is materially there, and the  verse is just referring to the state of the earth
and the heavens when the creation of their  form and function as we recognize them
today – or at least as they recognize them in  the time period in which genesis 1 was written.
And so this is not creation ex nihilo by any  stretch of the imagination. Now 2 Maccabees
7:28 is from a much later time period. We are in  the second century – second, first century BCE,
maybe even in the first century CE – but we have a  more Greco-Roman worldview influencing the author
here. But the mother says to one of the sons, you  know, look at the the heavens and the earth or the
the sun, and I don't remember exactly  what the wording is there, but she says,
and know that they were not made from what is,  and the the phrase there in greek is ουκ εξ οντων,
not from the being, and onton, the being, is  sometimes interpreted to mean existence. So this
refers to things not being made from that which  exists, in other words, made out of nothing. But
that's not a good reading here because this phrase  is used elsewhere in Greek literature to refer to
sexual procreation among humans and  it reflects a more Aristotelian view
of being and non-being as two different states  in which matter could exist. The non-being didn't
refer to non-existence, it referred to not having  form and function, and to give something form and
function – to make it recognizable – was to move  it from the realm of the non-being into the realm
of the being. In other words, this is probably  – most likely 2 Maccabees 7:28 referring to
this Aristotelian idea of the earth not being made  from material that already had form and function,
but being made from material that did not.  I'm going to put up some recommended reading   on the screen here, so if you want to track down  some of this scholarship a little more, including
some more recent scholarship that doesn't agree  totally with me, but is trying to take seriously
some of the objections that have been raised over  the last few decades regarding creation ex nihilo   in the Bible. So if you're looking for  more reading, go ahead and check it out.
